questions.question: What helps reduce your reaction time?

options.text: Ride slower than the speed limit.
Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.
Pull in the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes to reduce reaction time. This is especially important in areas where hazards are likely.

questions.question: What should you do when going through a curve?

options.text: Always stay in the same part of the lane.
Always stay in the left part of the lane.
Always stay in the right part of the lane.
Adjust your position based on road and traffic conditions.

questions.correctAnswerText: Adjust your position based on road and traffic conditions.
questions.explanation: Road and traffic conditions change. Be ready to change your lane position as needed. The best path through a curve may not match the road's curve.

questions.question: What color is a warning sign?

options.text: Yellow with black letters or symbols
Blue with white letters or symbols
White with black letters or symbols
White with red numbers

questions.correctAnswerText: Yellow with black letters or symbols
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black letters or symbols. They tell riders about upcoming road hazards.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders position themselves in a group?

options.text: At the front of the group.
Just behind the leader.
Near the back of the group.
At the very back of the group.

questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This keeps them from having to chase the group. More experienced riders behind them can also keep watch.

questions.question: When do most motorcycle crashes happen?

options.text: At high speeds.
After riding for a long time.
Far from home.
On short trips close to home.

questions.correctAnswerText: On short trips close to home.
questions.explanation: Most motorcycle crashes happen on short trips less than five miles long at speeds under 30 miles per hour.

questions.question: How much more likely are helmeted riders to survive a crash?

options.text: Two times more likely
Three times more likely
Eight times more likely
Ten times more likely

questions.explanation: Wearing a helmet makes you three times more likely to survive head injuries in a crash compared to not wearing one.

questions.question: Which is NOT a requirement for a good helmet?

options.text: Meets U.S. DOT standards.
Fits snugly.
Has no visible damage.
Was worn in a previous crash.

questions.correctAnswerText: Was worn in a previous crash.
questions.explanation: A good helmet must meet DOT standards, fit snugly, and have no visible damage. Replace any helmet that was worn during a crash.

questions.question: What is the best lane position when following a car?

options.text: The left portion of the lane.
The center of the lane.
The right portion of the lane.
Either the left or right portion.

questions.explanation: Ride in the center of the lane so the driver can see you in their rearview mirror. Drivers check rearview mirrors more often than side mirrors, so this position makes you more visible.

questions.question: Do you need hearing protection when riding?

options.text: No, a helmet is enough.
Yes, even with a helmet.
Only on windy days.
No, not when carrying a passenger.

questions.explanation: Engine and wind noise can damage your hearing even with a helmet. Use hearing protection to guard your hearing while still hearing important sounds like horns and sirens.

questions.question: Which is a poor reason to use your horn?

options.text: A driver is too close to the car ahead.
Someone is sitting in a parked car.
You want people to notice your motorcycle.
You are passing a pedestrian in the street.

questions.correctAnswerText: You want people to notice your motorcycle.
questions.explanation: Use your horn to warn vehicles or pedestrians who might enter your path. Sound your horn when passing a car too close to another vehicle, when someone is in a parked car, or when passing pedestrians. Do not use it just to get attention.

questions.question: What does this signal mean?

options.text: Rest stop
High beams on
Turn right
Hazard

questions.explanation: Signals help riders communicate in groups. When the lead rider extends their right leg, it means there is a hazard on the right side of the road.

questions.question: When preparing to pass a vehicle on the left, you should ride on the left side of your lane because:

options.text: The right side could be slippery.
It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
People don't usually expect to be passed on their left.
It places you in the rearview mirror of the car in front.

questions.correctAnswerText: It gives you the best view of hazards in the next lane.
questions.explanation: Ride on the left side of your lane when preparing to pass. This position improves your sight line and makes you more visible to oncoming traffic.

questions.question: Usually, you should maintain a minimum following distance of _____ seconds.

options.text: One
Two
Three
Four

questions.explanation: Keep a minimum following distance of two seconds. Increase this to at least three seconds if conditions are not ideal.

questions.question: When a vehicle is passing you on your left, you should:

options.text: Move as far to the right as possible to help them pass.
Move to the shoulder to help them pass.
Ride in the center of your lane.
Ride on the left side of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. Riding near the passing vehicle increases collision risk. Riding on the far side may cause them to merge back too soon. Stay centered.

questions.question: If a small animal enters your lane in traffic, you should:

options.text: Swerve into other lanes to avoid hitting it.
Switch lanes as quickly as possible.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare the animal.

questions.explanation: Avoid hitting an animal when you can do so safely. In traffic, stay in your lane. Swerving into another lane can cause you to hit another vehicle. Hitting a small animal is safer than hitting another car.

questions.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: Both brakes provide equal stopping power.
The front brake is stronger than the rear brake.
The rear brake is stronger than the front brake.
Use only the front brake when stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake is stronger than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake is more powerful and provides about 70 percent of total stopping power. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: Motorcycles are hard to see at night. To be safer, a rider should:

options.text: Slow down when riding at night.
Sound the horn repeatedly at night.
Not ride at night.
Stay directly in front of another vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down when riding at night.
questions.explanation: Safe night riding includes: slowing down, increasing following distance, using other vehicles' lights to see ahead, using your high beam (unless near other traffic), and adjusting your lane position as needed.

questions.question: When riding, you should:

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn only your head and eyes to look where you are going.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn only your head and eyes to look where you are going.
questions.explanation: In turns, look ahead by turning only your head. Keep your knees against the gas tank to help balance. Bend your arms slightly when holding the handgrips.

questions.question: When riding at night, the minimum following distance should be:

options.text: Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.
Five seconds.

questions.explanation: At night, seeing is harder and judging distance is harder. Keep at least three seconds of distance from the vehicle ahead. You need extra time to notice when they brake and to stop.

questions.question: When riding in a group, the best formation is generally:

options.text: Pairs.
A staggered formation.
A single-file line.
A pyramid formation.

questions.explanation: Use a staggered formation when riding in a group. Switch to single-file when turning, riding curves, or entering or exiting highways.

questions.question: Most motorcycles have rounded mirrors. What do these mirrors do?

options.text: They are easy to get used to right away.
They make cars look closer than they really are.
They show a narrow view of the road.
They make cars look farther away than they really are.

questions.correctAnswerText: They make cars look farther away than they really are.
questions.explanation: Rounded mirrors show a wider view than flat mirrors. They also make objects look farther away than they actually are. Practice judging distances with rounded mirrors if you are not used to them.

questions.question: In a group ride, where should inexperienced riders be placed?

options.text: At the front of the group.
Just behind the lead rider.
At the back of the group.
Anywhere within the group.

questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way, experienced riders can watch them from behind.

questions.question: On a two-lane highway, how should a group of motorcycle riders pass other vehicles?

options.text: In pairs.
One at a time.
In a single-file line.
On the shoulder.

questions.explanation: On a two-lane road, only one rider should pass at a time. The lead rider should finish passing before the next rider passes.

questions.question: What guarantees that another driver sees you?

options.text: Eye contact
Using a turn signal
Following another vehicle
Nothing

questions.explanation: Nothing guarantees that a driver sees you. It is safest to assume that any vehicle can enter your path.

questions.question: When a group exits a highway, which riding formation should be used?

options.text: Staggered
Single-file
Paired up
Riding three across a lane

questions.explanation: A staggered formation is usually best for group riding. However, switch to single-file when taking curves, turning, or entering or exiting a highway.

questions.question: Which formation is best when a group of riders enters a curve?

options.text: Pyramid
Staggered
Single-file
Compressed

questions.explanation: A staggered formation is usually best for group riding to keep riders close while giving each rider space. Use single-file formation when taking curves, turning, or entering or exiting a highway.

questions.question: If a rider must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, what should they do?

options.text: Do one action, then the other.
Do both actions at the same time with extra braking pressure.
Do both actions at the same time, focusing mainly on swerving.
Do neither action.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action, then the other.
questions.explanation: You need good grip to swerve safely. Do not brake and swerve at the same time. Instead, do one action first and then the other.

questions.question: What does an integrated braking system do?

options.text: Applies partial rear braking when the front brake is applied.
Applies partial front braking when the rear brake is applied.
Applies equal braking to both front and rear brakes when either is applied.
Learns and remembers how hard the rider brakes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Applies partial front braking when the rear brake is applied.
questions.explanation: An integrated braking system is a type of linked braking system. When the rear brake is used, partial front braking is also applied. Check your owner's manual for details about your motorcycle's braking system.

questions.question: Who should set the pace in a group of riders?

options.text: The leader
The riders just behind the leader
The rider in back
The oldest rider

questions.explanation: The last rider should set the pace for the group. This ensures that no riders are left behind.

questions.question: What does this hand signal mean?

options.text: Plans to turn left.
Is about to stop.
Plans to turn right.
Is about to slow down.

questions.explanation: A hand signal is used instead of turn signals. When a rider's left arm is bent at the elbow and pointing upward, it means the rider plans to turn right or change lanes to the right.
